body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Sanctuary of Aphrodite Paphia. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

The Sanctuary of Aphrodite Paphia was a sanctuary dedicated to the goddess Aphrodite in ancient Palaepaphos on Cyprus, near the modern village of Kouklia. It was founded in the 12th century BC in the aftermath of the Late Bronze Age collapse.
It is located at the mythical birthplace of Aphrodite and in later antiquity was internationally renowned as the principal sanctuary of the cult of Aphrodite.

The Sanctuary operated continuously for over fifteen centuries, evolving into a major pan-Mediterranean religious center during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods before its ultimate decline in the late 4th century AD.

The site comprising the entire city of Palaepaphos (Old Paphos) is also referred to as "Kouklia-Palaepaphos" to further differentiate it from the nearby city of Nea Paphos (New Paphos) founded in the 4th century BC, the two were frequently confused by ancient authors.
The archaeological site of the Sanctuary was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980 under the name "Aphrodite's Sanctuary at Kouklia village" due to its historical religious significance.
History
Scholarly inquiry into the origins of cultic activity at Kouklia-Palaepaphos relies on architectural remains, epigraphic findings, and classical literary traditions.

It initially functioned as the urban cult center for the city-state of Paphos, whose homonymous seat, later renamed Palaepaphos, had been established 500 years earlier in the Bronze Age, around 1700 BC, as a coastal gateway and maritime trading hub specializing in the export of copper.
Coastal transformations and silting deprived Palaepaphos of its harbor some time prior to the 4th century BC, prompting the establishment of Nea Paphos as the polity’s main port.

During the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, pilgrims had to approach the Sanctuary of Aphrodite on foot from Nea Paphos or by overland routes in the interior hinterland rather than arrive directly by ship as they had when the harbor was still usable.
Archaeology
Early excavations

Early archaeological investigations at the Paphos sanctuary began with the British Cyprus Exploration Fund in 1887, 1888, followed by fieldwork in 1950 led by Terence B. These mid-twentieth-century excavations uncovered Late Bronze Age stratified deposits beneath later Roman and medieval structures, yielding wheelmade Late Cypriot pottery alongside copper slag.
Literary references
The Homeric Hymns written between 7th-4th centuries BC and spuriously ascribed to Homer in antiquity mention the sanctuary in Hymn 5 to Aphrodite:
She went to Kypros, to Paphos, where her precinct is and fragrant altar, and passed into her sweet-smelling temple.

Palaipaphos, which last is situated at about ten stadia above the sea, has a mooring-place, and an ancient temple of Aphrodite Paphia. Then to the promontory Zephyria, with a landing-place, and to another Arsinoe, which likewise has a landing-place and a temple and a sacred precinct.
And at a little distance from the sea is Hierokepis. Then to Paphos, which was founded by Agapenor, and has both a harbor and well-built temples.

It is sixty stadia distant from Palaiphaphos by land, and on this road men together with women, who also assemble here from the other cities, hold an annual procession to Palaipaphos... Then to a city Soloi, with a harbor and a river and a temple of Aphrodite and Isis.

After the capture of Troy the storm that overtook the Greeks on their return home carried Agapenor and the Arkadian fleet to Kypros, and so Agapenor became the founder of Paphos, and built the sanctuary of Aphrodite at Palaipaphos (Old Paphos).
Up to that time the goddess had been worshipped by the Kyprians in the district called Golgoi.
Tacitus described the altar and aniconic black stone worshipped at the sanctuary as the simulacrum of Venus:
Blood may not be shed upon the altar, but offering is made only with prayers and pure fire. The altar is never wet by any rain, although it is in the open air.

The representation of the goddess is not in human form, but it is a circular mass that is broader at the base and rises like a turning-post to a small circumference at the top. The reason for this is obscure.
